historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: NMDA receptor antagonists (adamantane branch)

starting.description: A reported, unexpected improvement of Parkinson symptoms during antiviral amantadine use opened CNS medicinal-chemistry work on adamantanes; the known CNS-active drug became a comparator in testing the already synthesized dimethyl analogue. The sources do not explicitly establish that the individual patient case prompted the inventors' selection of that analogue.

inspiration.description: Observed clinical Parkinson effects of the synthetic antiviral amantadine and comparative biological effects of its existing synthetic dimethyl analogue. The clinical case is a family-level historical starting point; the specific reason Merz selected the analogue is not documented by these accounts.

steps.description: Before the Parkinson case, an Eli Lilly program prepared the dimethyl compound as an intermediate in work on a potential hypoglycemic sulfonylurea; the compound itself lacked the sought blood-sugar effect.
A patient's unexpected improvement while receiving antiviral amantadine was followed by clinical investigation and, according to a later history, a CNS medicinal-chemistry line involving adamantanes.

In an anti-Parkinson CNS investigation, the patent reported comparative animal effects for the already available dimethyl analogue and known active amino-adamantane. The 1978 U.S. document claims 1972 and 1973 priorities; the 1972 German filing's experimental contents have not been independently checked.

The 1999 retrospective connects preclinical NMDA findings with a 1989 application for cerebral ischemia and Alzheimer dementia; researchers later characterized the existing compound's channel-blocking kinetics. Some studies cited by that retrospective postdate 1989 and cannot have motivated that filing.

design.description: Chemists had prepared an aminoadamantane bearing two extra methyl groups for a different program. Investigators later prepared and compared its hydrochloride with known CNS-active aminoadamantane, pursued a CNS use, and later researchers characterized its NMDA channel-blocking behavior and implications of the two methyl groups. The sources do not establish that the original methyl substitutions were designed for NMDA antagonism.

circumstances.description: The clinical Parkinson response reported during amantadine influenza prevention was unexpected; the patent's comparative CNS experiments on the known compounds were planned. This does not assert that the first observation of the dimethyl analogue's CNS effects was accidental.

limits: The assignment covers the adamantane NMDA-antagonist branch represented by memantine; ketamine and other chemical branches are out of scope, and the conclusion should not be generalized to NMDA antagonists as a whole.

The patient observation concerns amantadine; the patent describes the pre-existing dimethyl analogue and comparative animal effects. Direct evidence that the individual case caused its selection is missing.
conflicts: S1 describes the 1972 patent application as demonstrating CNS activity, whereas S4 says that the 1972 filing contained no examples, details, or studies. These may distinguish a therapeutic claim from experimental disclosure, but the unread German filing prevents resolution. The 1978 U.S. patent has animal data and claims 1972 and 1973 priorities; its data are not automatically assigned to the 1972 document.

S2 mentions a 1968 patent while S1, S3 and S4 place preparation of the dimethyl compound in a 1963 publication. A later patent date does not by itself establish first synthesis; the primary 1963 paper and the patent referred to by S2 were not read.
gaps: The full Gerzon et al. 1963 original synthesis paper and Bormann 1989 original NMDA report were located by DOI and PMID but not read; the clinical 1969 Schwab report was read only in abstract.
The patent does not explicitly identify what prompted its investigators to select the existing dimethyl compound or attribute their selection to the individual amantadine-treated patient.
The original 1972 and 1973 German priority documents have not been read, and the source of the precise 1968 patent date in S2 has not been resolved.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Improvement of Parkinson symptoms during amantadine use for influenza helped stimulate adamantane CNS development.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: This does not prove that the same patient observation directly caused selection of memantine.
